blocks.tex:
The four-vertex theorem says that the curvature of a simple closed plane curve
that is not a circle has at least two local maxima and two local minima. Its
converse, that every such function on the circle is the curvature of a simple
closed curve, was proved by Gluck~\cite{Gluck1971} for strictly positive
curvature and by Dahlberg~\cite{Dahlberg2005} in general; see
\cite{DGPV2007} for the history.

The four-vertex theorem has many discrete versions
\cite{Musin2004,OvsienkoTabachnikov2001,Sedykh1997,Tabachnikov2000,Dahlberg2008,Pak2010}.
In the one studied here the curvature at a vertex of a polygon is the
reciprocal radius of the circle through that vertex and its two neighbours.
Let $P$ be a convex $n$-gon, $n\ge 4$, with vertices $x_1,\dots,x_n$ in cyclic
order. Following Tabachnikov, call $P$ \emph{coherent} if for every $i$ the
center of the circle through $x_{i-1},x_i,x_{i+1}$ lies inside the angle of
$P$ at $x_i$. If $P$ is coherent and no four consecutive vertices lie on a
circle, then the cyclic sequence $r_1,\dots,r_n$ of the radii of these circles
has at least two local maxima and two local minima. This is due to
Musin (see \cite{Tabachnikov2000,Musin2004}); Dahlberg~\cite{Dahlberg2008}
proved a version for simple, not necessarily convex polygons, extending
Bilinski's result for convex polygons with obtuse angles~\cite{Bilinski1963}.

In~\cite[Problem~2]{Tabachnikov2008} Tabachnikov posed the converse: a cyclic
sequence $r_1,\dots,r_n$ with at least two local maxima and two local minima
should be the radius sequence of a coherent convex polygon. Pak remarks
that he is not aware of a nontrivial discrete version of the converse
four-vertex theorem \cite[\S21]{Pak2010}. We prove Tabachnikov's conjecture.

Local extrema are counted as by Dahlberg \cite{Dahlberg2008}. A
\emph{plateau maximum} of a cyclic sequence is a maximal run of equal
consecutive terms, not the whole sequence, whose two outside neighbours are
both strictly smaller. Plateau minima are defined in the same way. Two
extrema are \emph{distinct} if their runs are disjoint.

blocks.label: thm:main
blocks.title: thm:main
blocks.body:
Let $n\ge 4$ and let $r_1,\dots,r_n>0$ be a cyclic sequence with at least two
distinct plateau maxima and two distinct plateau minima. Then there is a
simple, strictly convex, coherent polygon $x_1,\dots,x_n$, listed
counterclockwise, whose circle through $x_{i-1},x_i,x_{i+1}$ has radius $r_i$
for every $i$.

lean.name: Gluck.Discrete.tabachnikov_converse_geometric
lean.code:
theorem tabachnikov_converse_geometric [NeZero n] (hn : 4 ≤ n) {r : ZMod n → ℝ}
    (hr : ∀ i, 0 < r i) (hext : IsPlateauTwoMaxTwoMin r) :
    ∃ v : ZMod n → ℂ, IsCoherentConvexPolygon v ∧
      ∀ i, vertexCircumradius v i = r i :=
  (tabachnikov_converse hn hr hext).imp fun _ h ↦ ⟨h.1, h.2.1⟩

lean.name: Gluck.Discrete.IsCoherentConvexPolygon.signedMengerR2_eq_inv_of_radii
lean.code:
lemma IsCoherentConvexPolygon.signedMengerR2_eq_inv_of_radii
    {v : ZMod n → ℂ} {r : ZMod n → ℝ} (h : IsCoherentConvexPolygon v)
    (hrad : ∀ i, vertexCircumradius v i = r i) (i : ZMod n) :
    signedMengerR2 (v (i - 1)) (v i) (v (i + 1)) = 1 / r i := by
  simpa only [one_div_one_div, SignedMengerProfile_apply] using
    congrArg (fun x : ℝ ↦ 1 / x) ((h.vertexCircumradius_eq_inv i).symm.trans (hrad i))

lean.name: Gluck.Discrete.IsCoherentConvexPolygon.not_concyclic4_of_radius_ne
lean.code:
lemma IsCoherentConvexPolygon.not_concyclic4_of_radius_ne
    {v : ZMod n → ℂ} {r : ZMod n → ℝ} (h : IsCoherentConvexPolygon v)
    (hrad : ∀ i, vertexCircumradius v i = r i) (i : ZMod n)
    (hne : r i ≠ r (i + 1)) :
    ¬ Concyclic4 (v (i - 1)) (v i) (v (i + 1)) (v (i + 2)) :=
  fun hcon ↦ hne ((hrad i).symm.trans
    ((vertexCircumradius_eq_of_concyclic i (h.2.2 i).1 (h.2.2 (i + 1)).1 hcon).trans
      (hrad (i + 1))))

blocks.tex:
Strict convexity means that every vertex lies strictly to the left of every
edge not incident to it; coherence places each circumcenter in the open
vertex angle. The same polygon has signed Menger curvature $1/r_i$.
Moreover, whenever $r_i\ne r_{i+1}$, the four vertices
$x_{i-1},x_i,x_{i+1},x_{i+2}$ do not lie on a common circle, independently of
whether other adjacent radii are equal.




Two distinct plateau maxima already force two distinct plateau minima, and
conversely (\ref{lem:dfv-plateau}), so either half of the hypothesis
suffices.

\href{../figures/tabachnikov-example.svg}{Illustration: tabachnikov-example}

A coherent convex octagon realizing the curvatures
$(3,1.2,2.2,0.8,2.6,1,1.6,0.7)$, and its eight circles through consecutive
vertex triples, whose centers lie inside the vertex angles. Computed
numerically and checked to double precision.


\ref{fig:example} shows an example. The theorem is sharp:

blocks.label: cor:iff
blocks.title: cor:iff
blocks.body:
Let $n\ge4$ and let $r_1,\dots,r_n>0$ be nonconstant. Then $r$ is the radius
sequence of a coherent convex polygon if and only if $r$ has two distinct
plateau maxima and two distinct plateau minima.

lean.name: Gluck.Discrete.tabachnikov_radius_characterization
lean.code:
theorem tabachnikov_radius_characterization [NeZero n] (hn : 4 ≤ n) {r : ZMod n → ℝ}
    (hr : ∀ i, 0 < r i) (hnc : ¬ ∃ c, ∀ i, r i = c) :
    (∃ v : ZMod n → ℂ, IsCoherentConvexPolygon v ∧
      ∀ i, vertexCircumradius v i = r i) ↔ IsPlateauTwoMaxTwoMin r := by
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨v, hv, hrad⟩
    have hnoncircle : ¬ Concyclic v := by
      intro hcircle
      obtain ⟨c, hc⟩ := exists_constant_signedMengerProfile_of_concyclic_positiveOrientation
        hv.1 hcircle hv.positivePolygonOrientation
      apply hnc
      refine ⟨1 / c, fun i ↦ ?_⟩
      rw [← hrad i, hv.vertexCircumradius_eq_inv i, hc i]
    have hfv := dahlberg_discrete_four_vertex_E2 hn v hv.1 hv.2.2.dahlbergRegular hnoncircle
    have hpos : ∀ i, 0 < SignedMengerProfile v i := fun i ↦
      signedMengerR2_pos_iff_crossR2_pos.mpr (hv.positivePolygonOrientation i)
    have hinv := dahlbergFourVertex_inv_of_pos hpos hfv
    have heq : ∀ i, r i = (SignedMengerProfile v i)⁻¹ := by
      intro i
      rw [← hrad i, hv.vertexCircumradius_eq_inv i, one_div]
    exact (dahlbergFourVertex_congr heq hinv).hasTwoPlateauMaxRuns_and_min
  · exact tabachnikov_converse_geometric hn hr

deps.title: Exact characterization of positive nonconstant circumradii
deps.label: mf:core-iff

blocks.tex:
One direction is \ref{thm:main}. Conversely, a coherent convex
polygon is simple, and its circumcenters lie in the closed vertex sectors,
which is Dahlberg's local regularity \cite[Definition~1]{Dahlberg2008}. It is
not inscribed in a circle, since otherwise all the circles through
consecutive triples would coincide and $r$ would be constant. Dahlberg's
discrete four-vertex theorem \cite[Theorem~1]{Dahlberg2008}, whose extrema
are plateau extrema with distinct runs, gives the two maxima and two minima.
Only its convex case is needed here, since the polygon is strictly convex.
The formalization includes this forward implication and the equivalence.

blocks.label: rem:wording
blocks.title: The wording of the problem
blocks.body:
Read with strict extrema, $r_{i-1}<r_i>r_{i+1}$, Tabachnikov's hypothesis
is a special case of \ref{thm:main}. Read with weak extrema,
$r_{i-1}\le r_i\ge r_{i+1}$, the statement is false: $r=(2,1,1,1)$ has the
weak local maxima $r_1,r_3$ and minima $r_2,r_4$ but one plateau maximum, so
by \ref{cor:iff} it is not a radius sequence. The constant
sequence, covered by neither reading, is realized by the regular $n$-gon.
Tabachnikov's non-concyclicity hypothesis holds for our polygon exactly when
$r_i\ne r_{i+1}$ for all $i$: one implication was just noted, and if
$r_i=r_{i+1}$ in a coherent convex polygon, the circles at $x_i$ and $x_{i+1}$ share the chord
$x_ix_{i+1}$, the radius and the side of their centers, so they coincide.

blocks.tex:
\ref{sec:method} explains the construction informally; the proof
occupies \ref{sec:setup}--\ref{sec:constructions} and
\ref{sec:elimination}. \ref{sec:continuity} shows that the
polygon can be chosen to depend in a $C^1$ way on the data near every
nonconstant admissible sequence (\ref{thm:local}), but that a global
continuous choice does not exist, even along a path of admissible
nonconstant hexagon data (\ref{thm:hexagon}); the obstruction is the
radius of the smallest enclosing circle. \ref{thm:main},
\ref{thm:local} and~\ref{thm:hexagon} are formalized in Lean~4 with Mathlib
\cite{GluckLean}; the theorem cards link their formal statements.

Tabachnikov also conjectured a converse for the radii of the circles tangent
to three consecutive sides, the discrete four-vertex theorem of
Wegner~\cite{Wegner1994,Tabachnikov2000}. \ref{sec:side-tangent} proves this companion converse for inward
circles tangent to the three supporting lines, including their extensions.
It does not use the four-length system of the main theorem.
\ref{sec:discussion} gives counterexamples for turning-angle curvature
and for the naive mixed-sign converse, and asks for the additional
hypotheses needed in the latter case.
